how-dimensional-weight-is-billed.html.text:
← Dimensional weight calculator

How dimensional weight is billed, and why the box wins

Every parcel carrier bills the greater of two numbers: what your package weighs, and what the space it occupies is priced at. The second is dimensional weight, and for anyone shipping light or bulky goods it is almost always the one that wins. The arithmetic is simple, it is entirely in your control, and most sellers meet it for the first time on an invoice rather than before choosing a carton.

Open the free dimensional weight calculator

The arithmetic, in order

  1. Measure the packed carton, outside dimensions, in inches. Round each side to the nearest whole inch, which is what most carriers do before they multiply.
  2. Multiply length by width by height. That is the cube, in cubic inches.
  3. Divide the cube by your DIM divisor. The published US domestic figure has been 139; your agreement may say 166, 194 or 250.
  4. Compare that to the actual weight and take the larger, then round up to the next whole pound. That is your billable weight.

Worked example

A four pound item in a sixteen by twelve by ten inch carton is 1,920 cubic inches. At a 139 divisor that is a dimensional weight of 13.81 pounds, so the package bills at 14 pounds to move four pounds of goods. Ten pounds of that invoice is empty space. The break even cube is the actual weight times the divisor, or 556 cubic inches here, so any carton smaller than roughly eight by eight by eight would have billed on the goods instead. On this footprint the same ceiling is a packed height of 2.9 inches, which tells you plainly that the fix is a different box rather than better packing.

Common questions

How is dimensional weight calculated?

Multiply the length, width and height of the packed carton in inches to get cubic inches, then divide by the DIM divisor in your carrier agreement. That result is the dimensional weight in pounds. The carrier bills the greater of that figure and the package's actual weight, rounded up to the next whole pound. Most carriers round each side to the nearest whole inch before multiplying, so a 12.5 inch side is cubed as 13.

What is a good DIM divisor?

A higher one, because it divides the same cubic inches into fewer pounds. The published US domestic figure for the major parcel carriers has been 139. Negotiated accounts commonly carry 166, and 194 or 250 appear on higher volume agreements. If you ship light bulky goods, a better divisor is often worth more than a headline rate discount, because it changes the weight every single package is rated at rather than the price of a weight you were never going to hit.

Why does a light item cost so much to ship?

Because the box is what gets priced, not the item. A four pound item in a sixteen by twelve by ten inch carton is 1,920 cubic inches, which at a 139 divisor is a dimensional weight of 13.81 pounds and a billable weight of 14. Ten of those pounds are air. Nothing about the item changed; the carton decided the bill, and a smaller carton would have ended the penalty entirely.

How do I stop paying dimensional weight?

Get the cube below your actual weight multiplied by the divisor. That product is the break even: any carton under it bills on the goods instead of the space. For a four pound item at a 139 divisor the ceiling is 556 cubic inches, which is roughly an eight by eight by eight box. Right sizing cartons, using fewer sizes with less void fill, and shipping flat where the product allows are the three changes that move it.

What is girth, and why do carriers care about it?

Girth is the longest side plus twice each of the other two, which approximates the strap around measurement of the package. Parcel surcharge tables are written in it because it captures awkwardness in a single number. Past certain lengths and girths a package picks up an additional handling charge, then a large package surcharge with its own minimum billable weight, and past the maximum it is refused as a parcel and has to move as freight.

Is dimensional weight the same as freight class?

No, though they solve the same problem. Parcel carriers convert volume to weight with a divisor and bill the greater of that and the scale weight. Less than truckload freight instead sorts a shipment into a class band from its density in pounds per cubic foot, and handling, stowability and liability can move that class regardless of density. Use a divisor for anything that ships as a parcel and a density band for anything on a pallet.

Why it is worth doing in advance

The point of working it out before you list a product rather than after you ship one is that both levers are cheap in advance and expensive later. Carton sizes are a purchasing decision you make once and live with for thousands of shipments, and the DIM divisor is a line in an agreement you can ask about at renewal. Neither is available to you on the day the invoice arrives.

Shipping on pallets instead? Less than truckload freight prices on density bands rather than a divisor — the LTL freight class estimator covers that case.

Common questions

What is dimensional weight?

It is the weight a carrier assigns to the space your package takes up, so that a box of pillows does not travel for the price of a box of bolts. Take the cubic inches of the carton and divide by a number in the contract called the DIM divisor. The carrier then bills the greater of that figure and what the package actually weighs, rounded up to the next whole pound. A trailer runs out of room long before it runs out of payload, which is why the space is what gets priced.

What is a DIM divisor, and which one applies to me?

It is the constant that converts cubic inches into pounds, and it is the single most valuable number in a parcel agreement. A bigger divisor means a smaller dimensional weight and a cheaper bill. The published US domestic figure for the major carriers has been 139, but negotiated accounts routinely carry 166, 194 or 250, and the divisor can differ between ground and air on the same account. This page defaults to 139 and lets you change it, because the right answer is on your rate agreement rather than in any calculator.

Why is my shipping cost higher than the weight on the scale?

Because you are not being billed on the scale. If the carton prices above the goods, the dimensional figure wins and the difference is air you are paying to move. This page names that gap in pounds rather than leaving it as a ratio, because the number that changes a decision is how many pounds of nothing are on the invoice. A four pound item in a sixteen by twelve by ten inch carton bills at fourteen pounds at a 139 divisor: ten of those pounds are empty space.

What size box stops me paying for air?

Any box whose cube is below your actual weight multiplied by the divisor. The page works that ceiling out and states it in cubic inches, and where the footprint allows it, also as a packed height on the carton you already have. Sometimes the honest answer is that no height reaches it, because the length and width alone already price above the goods. In that case the page says so instead of telling you to pack a mug flat, since a smaller footprint is the only thing that would work.

Should I round the dimensions?

Usually yes, and the checkbox is on by default. Carriers measure each side and round it to a whole inch before multiplying, so a carton measuring twelve and a half inches on every side is cubed as thirteen. Rounding after the multiplication instead of before gives a different and smaller answer, which is how an estimate and an invoice end up disagreeing. Turn it off if your service prices on exact measurements.

What are the girth and surcharge warnings?

Girth is the strap-around measurement that parcel surcharge tables are written in: the longest side plus twice each of the other two. Above certain lengths and girths a package stops being ordinary and picks up additional handling, then a large package surcharge, then refusal as a parcel altogether. The page flags which band the carton falls in from its dimensions alone. It deliberately does not quote a dollar figure, because those amounts are rate card terms that change and would go stale here.

Does this work for several packages at once?

Yes, for identical ones. Each package is rated on its own and rounded up on its own, so the total is the per package billable weight times the count. That matters more than it sounds: adding the cubes together and dividing once would quietly lose the round up on every package, which is exactly the sort of small error that makes an estimate disagree with an invoice. If your cartons differ, run each configuration separately.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests. The arithmetic runs entirely in your browser and nothing about your packages is sent anywhere. The usage counter is a local, opt out tally of which features were used, never your dimensions or weights.

Are my numbers saved, and can I share them?

Your last entry is kept in this browser's local storage, so a refresh or a visit tomorrow restores it, and nothing is uploaded. Copy shareable link puts the same figures in the page's URL fragment, after the hash, so sending that link to a co packer or a 3PL rep opens this page with the identical package already worked out. A link takes priority over a saved draft when you open one.

vs-guessing-the-box-size.html.text:
← Parcel dimensional weight calculator

This calculator vs. guessing which box triggers the dimensional penalty

Picking "the smallest box that fits" by eye is the right instinct and the wrong unit. Dimensional weight is a ratio — cubic inches divided by a divisor from your rate agreement — and two cartons that look equally roomy can land on opposite sides of it. A guess can tell you a box fits; it cannot tell you it is billing you for air, or by how much.

This calculator works the ratio both ways: the billable weight your current carton produces, and the exact cube and packed height at which the penalty stops, so a packaging change is a number to hit instead of a hunch to repeat.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is this box billing me for air, and how much? This calculator's billable weight panel, which states the gap in pounds — not a ratio a guess could approximate.
What is the exact size that stops the penalty? The break-even cube and packed height the panel works out from your own divisor, in cubic inches and inches.
Did this carton just cross a surcharge threshold? The girth and longest-side flags, which a box that "looks fine" gives no warning about at all.
What does a run of ten identical cartons actually total? The per-package total, which rounds each package up on its own rather than averaging the run into one guess.
Check a box size now

No account and no upload: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the dimensions you type stay on this device.

Common questions

Why can't I just eyeball whether a box is too big?

Because the penalty is not about how the box looks, it is about a ratio you cannot see: cubic inches divided by a divisor, compared against the scale weight. Two boxes that look identically "roomy" to the eye can sit on opposite sides of that line — one billed on the goods, one billed on several extra pounds of air — and nothing about their appearance tells you which.

What does a guess get wrong that the math does not?

Three things: the exact pounds of air you are paying for, the precise cube and packed height at which the penalty stops, and whether the carton's girth or longest side has crossed into an additional-handling or oversize band. A guess can tell you a box seems fine; it cannot tell you it is 2 inches of height away from a cheaper bill, or that it just crossed a surcharge threshold.

Isn't "use the smallest box that fits" good enough?

It is the right instinct with no way to act on it precisely. Smallest-that-fits still leaves you not knowing whether you are 5 pounds of air under the actual weight or exactly on it, and it says nothing about the divisor on your specific account, which can be 139, 166, 194 or 250 depending on your contract. The instinct is correct; only the arithmetic behind it decides whether it saves money.

Does this replace checking with my carrier rep?

No. The divisor, the surcharge dollar amounts, and the rounding rule are contract terms that differ by carrier, service and account, and this calculator asks you for the divisor rather than assuming one. It replaces the guess about which box triggers the penalty, not the rate agreement itself.

What happens when I ship several packages at once?

A guess has no way to catch this at all: each package rounds up to the next whole pound on its own, so a run of ten cartons that each look "about right" can round up ten separate times. This calculator multiplies the per-package billable weight by the count, so the total reflects every round-up instead of one averaged guess.

vs-shipstation.html.text:
← Parcel dimensional weight calculator

This calculator vs. ShipStation's dimensional weight

ShipStation is a paid, subscription multi-carrier shipping platform: connect carrier accounts, create a shipment, and it rate-shops live prices across carriers — prices that already fold in each carrier's dimensional-weight charge for that box and destination. Its own published guidance on how dimensional weight and cubic rates work explains the mechanics; the tool itself prices a real shipment once you have one to price.

This calculator answers the question that usually comes before that: while you are still choosing a box, what does this carton actually bill at, how many pounds of that are air, and what is the exact cube and packed height at which the dimensional charge stops applying at all? It does not rate-shop or buy labels, and it needs no account, no carrier connection and no subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What will a specific carrier actually charge to ship this box to this address today? ShipStation — that is a real, rate-shopped quote across your connected carrier accounts, which this calculator does not produce.
What box size stops me paying the dimensional penalty at all? This calculator's break-even cube and packed height panel — a target to pack to, not a quote for one shipment.
How many pounds of this bill are air, on the box I already have? This calculator's billable weight panel states the gap directly, before any carrier account is involved.
I'm ready to buy a label and want the cheapest carrier for this shipment. ShipStation — comparing live carrier rates on a real shipment is its job, not this calculator's.
Do I need to sign up for anything to check a box size? This calculator: no. ShipStation is a paid subscription with a free trial, and a real rate needs a connected carrier account.
Check a box size now

Most sellers get use out of both, for different moments: this calculator while deciding on packaging before a run of a SKU ships, and a multi-carrier platform like ShipStation when it is time to actually rate-shop and label a shipment.

No account and no upload here: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the dimensions you type stay on this device.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ShipStation?

They answer different questions at different points in the job. ShipStation is a paid, subscription multi-carrier shipping platform: you connect carrier accounts, create a shipment, and it rate-shops live carrier prices, which already fold in each carrier's dimensional-weight charge for that specific box and destination. Its own published guidance walks through how dimensional weight and cubic rates are calculated. This calculator does not rate-shop, does not buy labels, and does not need a carrier account or a login — it answers the question that usually comes first, while you are still choosing a box: what does this carton bill at, how many pounds of that are air, and what is the exact size that stops the penalty? Decide the box here, then take it to ShipStation (or any carrier account) to actually rate-shop and ship it.

Is this page affiliated with ShipStation?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ShipStation or its parent company. ShipStation is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

Does ShipStation tell you the box size that stops the dimensional penalty?

Not as a standalone question. ShipStation shows you the rate a carrier charges for the box and weight you already entered on a real shipment — it is a rate-shopping and label tool, not a packaging worksheet. This calculator works the ratio backwards from a target: given your actual weight and DIM divisor, it names the exact cube in cubic inches and, where the footprint allows it, the packed height in inches at which the dimensional charge stops applying at all.

Do I need an account or connected carriers to use either tool?

For ShipStation, yes — it is a paid subscription product, priced by monthly shipment volume with a free trial and no permanent free plan, and getting a real rate means connecting at least one carrier account. This calculator needs neither: it is a free static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once it has loaded.
